clue.text: Confusion when letter from Greece gets delivered late with contents missing

indicators.note: with the contents gone, only the outside letters of each word remain

blocks.note: mu is the twelfth letter of the Greek alphabet
the first and last letters of 'delivered'
the first and last letters of 'late'

explanation.surface: A letter posted from Greece turns up late and empty, causing chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letter from Greece' sounds like post, but it means a Greek alphabet letter; 'with contents missing' applies to both 'delivered' and 'late', leaving DD and LE.
explanation.definitionFit: A muddle is a state of disorder or mix-up, a direct synonym for confusion.

clue.text: Surgeon's worried, squeezing opening of cut with sponge

indicators.note: worried can mean pulled about or harried, so the letters are disturbed into a new order
an opening is the start of something, so only its first letter is taken
to squeeze something is to press it inside, so one part is held within the other

blocks.note: the letters of 'surgeon' to be rearranged; the 's is just 'is'
the first letter of 'cut'

explanation.surface: An anxious surgeon holds a sponge to an incision during an operation.
explanation.walkthrough: The surgical sponge is a red herring: here 'sponge' is a verb, to live off others, and the 's after 'Surgeon' just means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To sponge is to cadge things from other people without paying, which is exactly what scrounging means.

clue.text: Take heart from Beano and Dandy, too

indicators.note: the heart is the centre, so only the middle letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the middle letter of the five-letter word
a dandy or swell is a fashionably dressed man

explanation.surface: The Beano and The Dandy are long-running British children's comics, and the clue sounds like taking encouragement from both.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make Dandy look like the comic title, but it is the old word for a showy dresser. Capitalising a word to disguise it is fair in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: 'As well' and 'too' are both adverbs meaning in addition or also, interchangeable in nearly any sentence.

clue.text: Belie crudely overshadowing good university's charm

indicators.note: done crudely means roughly handled, so the letters come out in a rough new order
to overshadow is to loom over and envelop, so one part wraps around the other

blocks.note: the letters of 'belie' to be rearranged
G is the standard abbreviation for good
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: Something crudely misrepresents the charm of a good university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belie' looks like part of the sentence's meaning but is only raw letters, and 'charm' is a verb here, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To beguile someone is to captivate or enchant them, so it is a verb synonym of charm.

clue.text: Great pub's diversified, importing beers regularly

indicators.note: something diversified has been varied or changed in form, so the letters take a new order
regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept
to import is to bring something inside, so one part goes within the other

blocks.note: the letters of 'pubs' to be rearranged
the second and fourth letters of 'beers'

explanation.surface: A great pub has broadened its range and now brings in beers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great' looks like praise for the pub, but it is the definition; the possessive 's on 'pub's' supplies a letter to the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Superb and great are both adjectives of high praise, meaning excellent or first-rate.

clue.text: Mocking extract from memoir on icon

indicators.note: an extract is a piece lifted from a longer text, so the letters run consecutively inside the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of 'memoir', all of 'on' and the start of 'icon'

explanation.surface: A satirical passage from a memoir written about some celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extract' pretends to be a literary excerpt, which it is, but of letters rather than prose.
explanation.definitionFit: Irony expresses something by saying its opposite, often with derision, so an ironic tone can be mocking.

clue.text: Clever move in dance

blocks.note: quick-witted, sharp
a step is a move, as in a course of action

explanation.surface: A smart manoeuvre performed in the middle of a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a neat manoeuvre on the dance floor; the two words actually join to make the dance itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The quickstep is a fast ballroom dance, so it is a specific example of a dance.

clue.text: Rush on hot curry when cold out

indicators.note: something that is out has gone away, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
taken as written before trimming
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: People rush out for a hot curry when the weather turns cold.
explanation.walkthrough: H for hot and C for cold are the tap labels; removing C from CURRY leaves URRY.
explanation.definitionFit: To rush and to hurry are both verbs meaning to move or act with great speed.

clue.text: Poem about Spanish gentleman abroad is unlike any other

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase; the definition is adjectival, read as 'is the one unlike any other'

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is placed round the other

blocks.note: an ode is a lyric poem
Don is the Spanish title for a gentleman
abroad means out and about, away from home

explanation.surface: A poem about a Spanish nobleman travelling abroad is unique.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' seems to belong to the gentleman's travels, but it is a separate piece meaning out and about.
explanation.definitionFit: The odd one out is the single member of a group that differs from all the rest.

clue.text: Jane's going out in trousers

indicators.note: going out suggests moving out of place, so the letters leave their order

blocks.note: the letters of the name with its S

explanation.surface: Jane heads out for the evening dressed in trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Going out' reads as a night out, but it tells you to rearrange the letters of 'Jane's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeans are denim trousers, so they are a particular kind of trousers.

clue.text: Last letter home has finally tragic element

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the word's tail is kept

blocks.note: Z is the final letter of the alphabet
being in means being at home
the last letter of 'tragic'

explanation.surface: A final letter sent home contains something tragic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last letter home' sounds like a soldier's farewell note, but it is Z followed by IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Zinc is a metallic chemical element, number 30 in the periodic table.

clue.text: Kneel awkwardly, installing new pet shelter

indicators.note: done awkwardly means clumsily, so the letters end up out of order
to install is to put something in place inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: the letters of 'kneel' to be rearranged
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone kneels clumsily while setting up a shelter for a new pet.
explanation.walkthrough: KNEEL rearranged as KEN...EL takes N in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A kennel is a small hut where a dog is housed, so it is a shelter for a pet.

clue.text: Student given help and support relaxed

blocks.note: L is a learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car
aid is help
to back someone is to support them

explanation.surface: A student who gets help and support feels at ease.
explanation.walkthrough: Student for L comes via learner, the L-plate shown by learner drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Laid-back is an informal adjective for someone calm, easygoing and unhurried.

clue.text: Former head of agency's upset getting sack

indicators.note: the head is the top or front, so only the first letter is used
upset means turned over, and in a down clue that flips the order upward

blocks.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
the first letter of 'agency'

explanation.surface: The agency's former chief is upset at being fired.
explanation.walkthrough: EX and A are put together and then turned over to read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack and to axe are both informal verbs for dismissing someone from a job.

clue.text: Fundamental shift?

blocks.note: first meaning: essential, of central importance
second meaning: the shift is one of the buttons on a keyboard, hence the question mark

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a basic change of direction; the question mark flags that shift is an example of the answer rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it means crucial or essential; as a noun it names a button on a keyboard, such as shift.

clue.text: Adamant about key American right to have a gun

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the others

blocks.note: firm means resolute, unyielding
E is one of the musical keys, A to G
A is the abbreviation for American
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone insists on the core American right to bear arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key American right' sounds like the Second Amendment, but splits into E, A and R, which FIRM wraps around.
explanation.definitionFit: A firearm is any portable gun, such as a rifle or pistol, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Craze to wane shortly

indicators.note: shortly read as cut short, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: to wane is to fade or dwindle

explanation.surface: A craze that is bound to die out soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' looks like 'soon', but it means shorten the word by its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A fad is a short-lived enthusiasm or fashion, the same thing as a craze.

clue.text: Serve up standard punishment

indicators.note: served up in a down clue means brought upward, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: par is the standard or norm, as in 'up to par'

explanation.surface: Hand out the usual penalty.
explanation.walkthrough: Rap as punishment comes from 'a rap on the knuckles' or 'take the rap'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rap is a rebuke or penalty, as in a rap on the knuckles or taking the rap for something.

clue.text: Drive quietly on sloping surface

blocks.note: to ram is to drive or force something in
P is piano, the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Steer gently on an incline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' suggests a car, but it is the verb for forcing something home; P for quiet comes from musical notation.
explanation.definitionFit: A ramp is an inclined plane joining two levels, which is literally a sloping surface.

clue.text: Backdrop ready at last, screen adaptation is going ahead

indicators.note: at last points to the end, so only the final letter is kept
an adaptation reworks the original into a new form, so the letters are rearranged
going ahead means moving in front, so this part is placed before the other

blocks.note: the letters of 'screen' to be rearranged
the last letter of 'ready'

explanation.surface: The set is finally finished, so the film version can proceed.
explanation.walkthrough: The film-set picture hides the order: the rearranged SCREEN goes ahead of the Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Scenery is the painted set behind actors on stage, which is what a theatrical backdrop is.

clue.text: Without doctor filling shift for a month

indicators.note: a filling goes inside something, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: no means without, as in 'no sugar'
MB is Bachelor of Medicine, a doctor's degree
to veer is to shift direction

explanation.surface: A rota left with no doctor to cover a month's shifts.
explanation.walkthrough: MB, the British medical degree, is a regular crossword doctor alongside DR and GP.
explanation.definitionFit: November is the eleventh month of the calendar year, so it is one particular month.

clue.text: Backsliding agent pockets bung

indicators.note: to backslide is to slip back the way you came, so the letters run in reverse

blocks.note: a rep is a sales agent or representative
in snooker, to pot a ball is to pocket it

explanation.surface: A corrupt agent relapses and pockets a bribe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bung' is British slang for a bribe, which the surface uses, but it also means a plug; 'pockets' is a verb meaning pots, not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A bung is a plug sealing a hole in a barrel or bottle, the same thing as a stopper.

clue.text: Official look at investing money after downward trend

indicators.note: to invest is literally to clothe or wrap, so the outer pieces surround another
after says which piece follows, fixing the order of the parts

blocks.note: a dip is a fall or downturn
lo is an old word for look, as in 'lo and behold'
taken as written
M is the abbreviation for money

explanation.surface: A finance official reviews investments following a market slump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Investing money' sounds financial, but investing here means clothing or wrapping one piece in another.
explanation.definitionFit: A diplomat is an official who represents a country abroad, so the word names a type of official.

clue.text: Clash with politician blocking international law

indicators.note: to block is to stand in the way, so one piece sits in the middle of the other

blocks.note: an MP is a Member of Parliament
I is the abbreviation for international
an act is a law passed by parliament

explanation.surface: A row breaks out with a politician obstructing international legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: An MP is a Member of Parliament, the British legislator, and a regular crossword politician.
explanation.definitionFit: An impact is a forceful collision, so as nouns impact and clash both mean a violent coming together.

clue.text: Yearned to sit around, getting rid of uniform with daft cap

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes it, so that letter is dropped
a cap sits on top, so in this down entry only the first letter is used

blocks.note: to lounge is to sit around idly
U is Uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the first letter of 'daft'

explanation.surface: Someone wished they could laze about, shedding their uniform for a silly hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daft cap' looks like a silly hat, but the cap of 'daft' is its first letter. LOUNGE loses U and gains D.
explanation.definitionFit: Yearned and longed are both past-tense verbs for having a strong wistful desire.

clue.text: Daughter stopping one bad habit gets counselling

indicators.note: to stop a gap is to plug it, so this piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a means one
D is the abbreviation for daughter
a vice is a bad habit

explanation.surface: A daughter trying to quit a bad habit receives counselling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stopping' looks like quitting the habit, but it means plugging D into the gap in A VICE.
explanation.definitionFit: Counselling is guidance given to someone, so as nouns it and advice share the same sense.

clue.text: Sailor's on way out of the country

blocks.note: AB is an able seaman, with the 's standing for 'is'
a road is a way

explanation.surface: A sailor is setting off to leave the country.
explanation.walkthrough: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor; in a down clue 'on' puts it above ROAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Abroad means in or to a foreign land, which is exactly being outside your own nation.

clue.text: Frank's in prison, having cheated

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison, and 'in prison' gives that word
to do someone is slang for cheating them, so 'did' means cheated

explanation.surface: Frank is behind bars because he was a cheat.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank looks like a man's name but is the adjective; the 's is 'is'. 'Did' is slang for swindled, as in 'I've been done'.
explanation.definitionFit: Candid and frank are both adjectives describing honest, open, straightforward speech.

clue.text: Splash out getting odds and ends with 25% off

indicators.note: a quarter off a four-letter word removes one of its letters

blocks.note: SP is starting price, the betting odds at the start of a race
taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: Someone splurges on bits and pieces bought at a quarter off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odds and ends' wants to be one phrase meaning bits and pieces, but splits into odds and ENDS.
explanation.definitionFit: To splash out is an informal idiom for spending money freely or extravagantly.

clue.text: Appropriate to house creative types in flat?

indicators.note: to house something is to give it a place inside, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: apt means suitable or appropriate
art men, playfully, are creative people

explanation.surface: It is fitting to put artists up in a flat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals the whimsical ART MEN for creative types; APT wraps round them.
explanation.definitionFit: An apartment is a self-contained set of rooms on one floor, the American word for a British flat.

clue.text: Suffered when a revolutionary leader died

blocks.note: taken as written
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born Cuban revolutionary
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: People suffered when a rebel chief passed away.
explanation.walkthrough: Che is the usual crossword revolutionary; D for died comes from genealogy and obituaries.
explanation.definitionFit: Ached and suffered are both past-tense verbs for having felt continuous pain or distress.

clue.text: I'm eager to change outside space for animal collection

indicators.note: to change something is to alter it, so the letters are put in a different order
outside means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go round the other piece

blocks.note: the letters of 'I'm eager' to be rearranged
an en is a printer's space, half an em wide

explanation.surface: Someone keen to make room outdoors for a collection of animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outside space' reads as a garden, but 'outside' is the wrapping signal and the space is EN, the printing measure.
explanation.definitionFit: A menagerie is a collection of wild animals kept for exhibition, often a travelling one.
